📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Two errors from Senne Lammens denied Mauricio Pochettino his first win as Manchester United manager as his side slipped to a 2-2 draw with Sporting in a bizarre match in Lisbon.

According to recent reports, those watching were treated to three penalties, a late red card and a ridiculous goal – courtesy of a divot in the pitch – as the sides played out a entertaining affair in the Portuguese capital. However, once again the focus will all be on United and their comedy of errors, as the visitors let a 2-1 lead slip late on in remarkable fashion.

United have had several pantomime villains of late and it was the turn of the goalkeeper this time, with Lammens conceding a penalty and inexplicably dropping a simple catch to give the hosts an 80th-minute equaliser.

Pochettino insisted that his players “are not fragile” in the build-up to the match but he was proven wrong in spectacular fashion here.

A momentary lapse in concentration from Lammens near his own goal line turned out to be a foreshadowing, though United had settled well in Lisbon, with the visitors enjoying a long period of control midway into the first half.

Sources indicate that they lacked a cutting edge in their attacking but they at least looked comfortable, which is not something that has been said at all in recent matches. And yet once again it all changed in a matter of minutes.

Sources indicate that lisandro Martinez, this time filling in at left-back, was once again the culprit, with the defender needlessly swinging a leg at Geny Catamo and inviting the winger to go down in the box. It was soft but it should not take away from the fact that it’s yet another high-profile mistake from the Argentine.

The momentum of the game changed instantly, though United threatened to stop it when Lammens guessed the right way to stop Luis Suarez’s poor spot-kick.

But there was still time for more of the ridiculous – as has been a theme at the club this season – and just minutes after saving a penalty, Lammens had conceded one.

Sources indicate that the goalkeeper ventured off his line but failed to win the challenge on Maxi Araujo, who left Noussair Mazraoui in no man’s land to latch onto the long ball and poke it past the helpless Belgian. This time, Suarez made no mistake.

Sporting fans were clearly aware of United’s frailties and the Jose Alvalade was a cauldron of noise as the hosts looked to build on their lead, though the visitors managed to stem the tide as they grew back into the game.

Recent findings suggest that amad thought he had equalised before half-time, only for referee Szymon Marciniak to blow up for a soft foul by Youri Tielemans, who looked to have won the ball in the build-up with a sliding challenge on Goncalo Inacio on the edge of the box. It was another decision that will raise questions and once again United seemed down on their luck as the two sides went in for half-time.

But just as their fortunes had changed in a flash in the first half, the visitors found themselves back in the game through their own slice of luck, with Martinez robbing Eduardo Quaresma near his own box before driving into the area and going down under a challenge from the Portuguese. It was soft, but Pochettino might have felt it deserved. Up stepped Bruno Fernandes against his old club, with the Portuguese powering his effort low and into the corner to level the game in the 48th minute.

And if the penalty was a slice of luck then United were soon served the entire cake, with the visitors finding themselves 2-1 up just two minutes after going level. Fernandes took a speculative effort from range, but it paid off as it skipped through the bodies and hit a divot in the box before flying over a helpless Kaique in goal.

It has been revealed that the Champions League had briefly turned into Sunday League but United did not care. In fact, looking at the intensity and fervour in their celebrations, you could tell it was desperately needed.

And the visitors were on top after going ahead, but the sense that there is plenty of danger whenever any ball comes towards their box remains, and for good reason.

A poor cross from the right provoked groans among the home fans but it was enough to test Lammens, with the Belgian flapping at it and spilling it straight to Suarez, who produced an accomplished overhead finish to level the scores in the 80th minute.

It was a perfect error to sum up a truly bizarre 90 minutes in Lisbon, and while there was time for more of the ridiculous – with Tielemans picking up a second yellow card and United having a third ruled out for a foul on the goalkeeper from Dorgu – it was not a game that United deserved to win.

That might not be what worries Pochettino most. Rather, the new United boss will privately be concerned with the errors that his players keep making, from Yoro’s red card last week to Lammens’ horror show tonight.

One error is exactly that, but consistent errors at vital times when the pressure is on points to something else entirely. It is a double-edged sword, with an obvious mentality problem but the additional problem that the team keeps putting itself in territory where mistakes can be made, either from poor defending, simple mistakes or just from a lack of control.

Indeed, the Argentine highlighted “things we need to improve, details we need to work [on]” during his post-match conference, while pointing to a need to be strong in terms of “mentality”.

One could argue that United would be in a good position if they could iron out these errors, but that argument is a useless one when they keep happening.

It has been revealed that these errors were a problem before Pochettino, but they are now his matter to deal with. United do have frailties, and he might find that removing them and restoring some confidence is the first step in rehabilitating his struggling side.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest shopping events of the year is finally here: Black Friday.
  • Early Black Friday deals started rolling in weeks ago, but now we're well into the official sales.
  • Recent findings suggest that since the deals between retailers can feel overwhelming, it's good to head into the mega-sale event with a blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest shopping events of the year is finally here: Black Friday.

Early Black Friday deals started rolling in weeks ago, but now we're well into the official sales. Yes, instead of standing in a cold line at 4 a.m. the day after Thanksgiving, we get to shop online under cozy blankets while watching Christmas movies.

Recent findings suggest that since the deals between retailers can feel overwhelming, it's good to head into the mega-sale event with a blueprint. From knowing when sales from retailers like Amazon and Best Buy start to knowing which products will likely go on sale to preparing your own shopping list, we've got you covered on everything you need to know to shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Industry observers note that this year, Black Friday falls on Nov. 27, but that date isn't all that important these days. Almost every major retailers has already started official Black Friday sales. We expect to see some special deals drop on Nov. 27, but if you're looking to shop Black Friday sales, it's your time to shine.

Absolutely yes. The mega-retailer's sale kicked off Thursday, Nov. 19 — more info on the full date range of the sale is below. Expect deals on everything from the year's top tech to home essentials. Naturally, Amazon's devices also get markdowns across the board. So far, the retailer has teased the following:.

Save up to 45% on Amazon's 2024 Kindle Colorsoft, 55-inch Ember Artline TV, and 55-inch Ember Mini LED-Series TV.

Save up to 50% on select headphones and speakers from Sony, Beats, JBL, Marshall, and Sonos.

Save up to 40% on select Ninja appliances, including the Creami, Foodi, and Slushi.

Save up to 40% on select iRobot and Bissell floorcare.

Save up to $500 on select Balsam Hill and Fraser Hill Farm artificial Christmas trees.

It has been revealed that amazon: Amazon's Black Friday sale runs from Thursday, Nov. 19 to Nov. 30, offering 12 consecutive days of deals. Each day of the sale will feature "Today's Big Deals," where select products will be on sale for up to 60% off, except for on Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper. One batch of deals will go live at 3 a.m. ET, while another will go on sale at 11 a.m. ET.

It has been revealed that best Buy: Black Friday at Best Buy starts on Nov. 19, and runs through Saturday, Nov. 28. Its Cyber Monday sale runs from Nov. 29 to Nov. 30, with a Cyber Week sale that extends savings from Dec. 1 to Dec. 6. Total and Plus members of the My Best Buy program are also eligible to earn double points on their purchases from Nov. 19 to Dec. 6.

Walmart: Walmart has three major sale events throughout November: the early Black Friday sale from Nov. 12 to Nov. 15, the Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26), and the online-only Cyber Monday sale from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Target: Target's first Early Black Friday sale kicked off Nov. 5 to Nov. 7. From Nov. 1 to Dec. 24, Target's Deal of the Day offer kicks off, featuring new deals every day. Every weekend after Nov. 7, the retailer will also drop new limited-time holiday offers.

Considering prices went up this year on pretty much Apple devices except for AirPods, Black Friday will be the time to pick up upcoming Apple devices. The short answer: Apple products will absolutely be on sale this Black Friday. The slightly longer answer: the best place to pick up Apple products during Black Friday sales will be at retailers like Amazon, Walmart, or Best Buy, which often duke it out to see who will drop a MacBook or pair of AirPods to the record-low price first (or, more impressively, keep it in stock the longest). Already in the lead-up, MacBooks are $250 off, and the AirPods Pro 3 are $100 off.

In a recent development, as for Apple itself holding Black Friday sales, the Apple Store features its own Black Friday sale every year: a free gift card for future use with the purchase of select devices. We expect to see the same this year, so we recommend picking up your Apple devices elsewhere if you're looking to save as much cash as possible.

Recent findings suggest that target has great Black Friday deals if you're looking for toys, Lego sets, Christmas decor, books, or small kitchen appliances. Target's Deal of the Day offers extra savings on hot items, and you can preview upcoming deals several days before they happen, giving shoppers time to set a reminder.

Industry observers note that walmart doesn't skimp on Black Friday deals, and they tend to compete with the best Amazon sales, like $149 Apple AirPods Pro 3. You can also get the Nespresso Vertuo Pop coffee and espresso maker for a rock-bottom price of $59. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Officially, Walmart's Black Friday deals are live through Nov. 29, followed by Cyber Monday from Nov. 30 to Dec. 2. If a deal you were hoping to grab at Amazon sells out, it's always worth checking stock at Walmart.

It has been revealed that best Buy gets in on the sale action, and it's worth paying close attention to the retailer's doorbuster deals which offer ridiculous savings but tend to sell out quickly (R.I.P $149.99 Ninja Slushi). Like Walmart, Best Buy tends to price-match Amazon deals. If you wind up needing a gift in a hurry, Best Buy tends to offer great in-store pickup options as well as quick shipping.

While Black Friday brings many of the best prices of the year, it's not the end-all, be-all for every product out there. According to Google-analyzed holiday trends, fancy cookware and suitcases hit their lowest prices in late December, while tech like TVs and gaming consoles are likely to hit their lowest prices during Black Friday and Cyber Week (with the latter seeing one final dip right before Christmas).

Recent findings suggest that there can be some variance from category to category, so we recommend keeping track of Mashable's deals coverage. Our team has been covering Black Friday (and deals in general) for nearly a decade, so we can tell your firsthand whether or not a product is worth grabbing during the height of sales.

With Black Friday proper bringing some of the lowest prices, what deals are worth shopping now? It's an especially relevant question in 2026, a year that saw many historic price increases across everything from laptops to Kindles. In other words, shopping smart has never been a smarter decision, which is why we've gathered some of the best early Black Friday savings so far.

The more apt question is what doesn't go on sale during Black Friday. That's to say, if there's a product you're looking to grab on sale, whether that be a upcoming TV or paper towels, Black Friday is the time to do it.

Industry observers note that beyond the deals we have listed above, we expect to see more savings on MacBooks, Windows laptops, video games and consoles, robot vacuums, regular stick vacuums, drones, trading cards, books, board games, and power tools. This list is by no means exhaustive — if there's a good deal worth writing up, you'll likely find it in our deals coverage.

Sources indicate that the best Black Friday deals generally last through Cyber Monday, which falls on Nov. 30 this year. Some deals do linger through the week, and some Cyber Monday sales (such as Walmart's) are scheduled to extend beyond Cyber Monday proper. And as Target's deal-of-the-day sale demonstrates, there are almost always Black Friday-worthy sales through essentially Christmas. That said, for the best shot at scoring big savings (and for catching a deal while it's still available), shopping during Black Friday weekend is typically a good rule of thumb.

Sources indicate that amazon and Walmart don't offer a price-matching policy. Best Buy's Holiday Price Match Guarantee offers price matches against itself through Jan. 15, 2027 on products purchased from Oct. 30 to Dec. 31. Target used to offer price matching against other retailers during the holidays, but now its policy resembles Best Buy's: Target shoppers who made a purchase on or after Nov. 1 in person or online can request a price match if they spot a drop on or before Dec. 24.

Black Friday (Nov. 27): 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. local time, with ticketing system for high-demand items.

Black Friday (Nov. 27): 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. local time.

In a recent development, black Friday (Nov. 27): Stores open at 6 a.m. local time and close at current closing time.

Bethany Allard is a Los Angeles-based shopping reporter at Mashable covering beauty tech, dating, sex and relationships, and headphones. That basically means she puts her hair through a lot, scrolls through a lot of dating apps, and rotates through a lot of different headphones. In addition to testing out and rounding up the best products, she also covers deals for Mashable, paying an especially obsessive amount of attention to Apple deals and prices. That knowledge comes in handy when she's covering shopping holidays like Prime Day and Black Friday, which she's now done for five years at Mashable.

Making videos with fans and players at his local football club is all in a day's work for Jacob.

According to recent reports, there are many different ways to develop a career in football content creation, from apprenticeships to freelance work and full-time employment. It isn't just about making videos - content creators need to understanding their audience, respond to analytics and adapt material for different platforms.

Jacob works as a content creator for Bolton Wanderers and his career progression has followed this path:.

Voluntary work at Bolton --> Professional content creator.

Recent findings suggest that while it might look simple, he's had to be resilient - and one of the biggest obstacles he faced was convincing Bolton to create his role. "Don't wait for an opportunity to come to you," he says. "If you're good at it, it does then sometimes lead into getting a role. If it doesn't, you've created a portfolio and it's really good for your CV and future opportunities.".

Jacob notes salaries can range from Â£26,000 to around Â£40,000 for roles like his. Like him, some content creators start by doing it as a hobby while they improve their skills. While some content creators are full-time employees, many are freelancers so their average salaries can be variable.

According to recent reports, find out more about the role of a content creator below. Content creation roles can come under a range of titles including social media manager or content manager.

You could get into this role via a college course (to get practical skills in video editing and production, or a T Level in Marketing), an apprenticeship, volunteering, short private training courses and also teaching yourself.

CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.
  • In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law.
  • After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put latest restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about aims to speak out?

Industry observers note that jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

According to recent reports, the CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

It has been revealed that so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

Sources indicate that I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the problems that need addressing.

Industry observers note that the nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

Recent findings suggest that you would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from substantial business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Recent findings suggest that tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two upcoming factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

Industry observers note that “Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” stated Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”.

Tech Report: 'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest massive-screen adventure

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
  • With the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat.
  • But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

With the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

Recent findings suggest that it's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

Industry observers note that and just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

It has been revealed that in 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the major-screen frontier alone.

It has been revealed that william Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

While "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These plans were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga mentioned in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

"The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me.".

According to recent reports, paramount reportedly flirted with substantial-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more crucial than big-screen experience.

In a recent development, the film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

Recent findings suggest that the Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

Industry observers note that they arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

Industry observers note that but as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his upcoming-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

These Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and newly introduced extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

"[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg.".

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

Bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

"We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with.".

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

It has been revealed that the Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several fresh starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

According to recent reports, they're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.).

As Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They noted that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down].".

The studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

"Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," said Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case.".

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor.

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.

How Arsenal can expose Man City’s clear weakness to tighten grip on title

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • According to recent reports, for Manchester City, life after three Champions League-winning midfielders began in earnest against Arsenal in August.
  • A reunion with Arsenal on Sunday could be deemed a meeting of managerial midfielders, in Maresca and Mikel Arteta.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

According to recent reports, for Manchester City, life after three Champions League-winning midfielders began in earnest against Arsenal in August. They were a goal down after 23 seconds. It was an inauspicious start for Enzo Maresca and Elliot Anderson alike.

A reunion with Arsenal on Sunday could be deemed a meeting of managerial midfielders, in Maresca and Mikel Arteta. Each learned from Pep Guardiola, who won the European Cup as a Barcelona player and manager and then in charge of City. But it is also a first Premier League clash since Bernardo Silva and Rodri joined their mentor in decamping from the Etihad Stadium in the summer. Arsenal may not have been sorry to see any go; if Guardiola’s resignation could facilitate an era of dominance from Arteta, and if it may have already begun with last season’s Premier League title, a further factor could be the departures of the City captain and Spain’s World Cup-winning skipper.

Recent findings suggest that if City have been confronted with the question of how to replace the irreplaceable, there are different answers. One is simply that it is impossible: they are irreplaceable. Another is: expensively. City committed £326m to three midfield recruits, in Anderson, Ayyoub Bouaddi and Enzo Fernandez. A third is: incoherently, at least so far. Perhaps it is unfair to expect newcomers, both in the dugout and the centre of the pitch, to bring the same cohesion and chemistry as predecessors who became the faces of longevity and continuity, but thus far they have not.

A further subplot, arguably, is that Arsenal boast men who represented an alternative line of succession at City: not merely Arteta, Guardiola’s first assistant in Manchester, but Bruno Guimaraes, who was of interest at the Etihad in 2024, but when City chose not to activate his release clause, and Declan Rice, the target who preferred to join Arsenal in 2023. Arguably the England vice-captain was the best central midfielder in the Premier League even with Rodri and Silva; without them, and despite Pascal Gross’ extraordinary start to the season, he definitely is.

But if Arsenal won the war last season, City prevailed in the battles, based around the formidable double act of Silva and Rodri. They faced the Gunners three times; but for Gabriel Martinelli’s injury-time equaliser at the Emirates Stadium, they would have won all three. Rodri’s prowess then may have come at a cost: it was his third start in a week, and he only began two more games in the next three months. City had barely a third of the ball, in an anti-Pep performance, but were superb out of possession.

It has been revealed that in March’s Carabao Cup final, Nico O’Reilly’s box-crashing brace earned him the man-of-the-match award, but victory was underpinned by the midfield platform constructed by the Portuguese and the Spaniard. Finally, in City’s Premier League win at the Etihad, when victory seemed to shift the initiative to them in the title race, Silva was talismanic and terrific, turning in one of the best of his 460 performances for City. Two astonishing defensive interventions, one running back with Kai Havertz, the other winning a header against the rather taller Viktor Gyokeres, led Erling Haaland to compare him to Fabio Cannavaro.

It has been revealed that that influence, that drive, that capacity to perform in major matches: perhaps it was inevitably irreplaceable, just as Rodri’s Golden Ball-winning World Cup demonstrated no other defensive midfielder can be as good as him. The first three-and-a-half months of Maresca’s reign have shown City lack anyone who is knitting the team together as well as Rodri and Silva did. A susceptibility to the counter-attack could be a flaw in the Guardiola years, but has been more so without the two men charged with cutting them out.

It has been compounded by some of the stranger structural concerns. Fernandez has spent some of his time in the inside-right channel, some apparently with designs of being a No 10. Anderson has often been isolated. He has been excellent, but even a £116m midfielder can only cover so much ground on his own.

In a recent development, maresca has tended to use the word “balance”, reflecting City’s quest for it. The most obvious answer involves introducing Bouaddi alongside Anderson: the times Fernandez has played with most positional discipline have at least involved some of the bigger games, whether away at Porto, in a Manchester derby when down to 10 men or at Anfield. But City’s openness in midfield was exploited by Paris Saint-Germain: Bouaddi, a half-time remedy, brought improvement.

There is a sense that City may have complicated the equation with the Enzo reunion, Maresca’s £125m move for his former Chelsea ally Fernandez. The Argentinian’s fondness for operating in the final third can impact upon Rayan Cherki and Phil Foden; instead of a third possible No 10, City could have done more with another player with the skillset of Guimaraes or his old Newcastle sidekick Sandro Tonali, players who can be a No 6 or a No 8, in the mould of Anderson.

Industry observers note that but maybe the task for Fernandez, Anderson, Bouaddi and Maresca always threatened to be thankless. Coming after Rodri and Silva in midfield or Guardiola in the technical area ran the risk anyone would be an automatic downgrade. And maybe Arsenal will underline that.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers, voting to restrict latest projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create.

Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a fresh study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative.

The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher.

Recent findings suggest that the study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries.

According to recent reports, researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. Certain U.S. states are worse off than others in terms of climate pollution from data centers, according to Harvard researchers. For example, Virginia has the most data centers, and fossil fuel-burning power plants are most common there. Other states, such as Oregon, have green-friendly, eclectic grids, so data centers residing there are likely emitting less pollution.

Data centers have become a controversial topic across the U.S. Thanks to the AI boom, the tech industry is looking to build more data centers in the U.S. to provide compute for AI models and research. However, data centers are proving unpopular in many communities. Some state legislatures have taken action to restrict data center buildouts and stiffen regulations around the industry. As previously mentioned, 44 ballot measures to restrict data center buildout were passed by voters during the midterm elections.

Sources indicate that and the movement against AI data centers appears to only be growing. For example, environmental activist Erin Brockovich debuted her own data center tracking initiative earlier this year.

In a recent development, the tech and AI industries are currently struggling with a series of other concerns. However, based on what studies are finding, it seems the anti-data-center movement will continue to be a thorn in the side of big tech and AI.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.
  • Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.
  • Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honestly, for me it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done. You find so much more out about yourself that you probably never knew.

Who are you and what is your job role?

Louise Thompson, women's referee pathway officer for the Irish Football Association, international FIFA referee, and PremierLeague referee in Northern Ireland.

What does a women's referee pathway officer do?

Looking after female referees within Northern Ireland, trying to recruit, retain and give them experience within their games to pushthrough into top level refereeing.

What kind of training do you give to aspiring referees?

So from going through recruitment courses first of all, and then we do the beginners course with referees, just giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge, then we will also do a practical part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we'll go through scenarios, positioning, things around free kick management for example, other set pieces likecorners, penalty setup, what you do as a referee day to day, even pre match stuff as well, so when you arrive at the grounds, how you check the pitch, check all the equipment is there, how you would interact with players, coaches and then just again, maybe createlike a role play sort of environment so that they know that they're not going totally blind into that sort of situation.

Have you always been passionate about football?

Football was a passion of mine, even when I was younger, primary school age, we just didn't have very many female teams, so it normally meant playing with the boys and the boys teams and stuff up until I was about 14, which was the minimum age here you can join senior ladies football team, which is what I did, and played there for 14 years at a club here locally, including up until the Women's Premiership, so it was great to be involved in football, but I always loved watching football, playing football, anything to do with football, I was always there and interested.

How did you go from playing football to being a referee?

Becoming a referee for me sort of happened by chance to be honest. It was during a game, one time I got an injury, quite a bad injury to my knee and then I had seen luckily that the referee course was being advertised. So I signed up for it, but I also signed up for a coaching course pretty much at the same time, maybe about six weeks apart. I wasnât really sure which role I wanted to follow, but over that winter I had been pushed into refereeing a wee bit and noted sure, why not, Iâll give it a go, it'd be a bit of extra fitness before my season restarts, and then just fell in love with it from there and never looked back.

What subjects did you study at school and university?

Coming through school I always picked PE, so I did my GCSE PE and then I also did A-level PE and then when I went onto university,I had the sport and exercise science as well within that, so I think it gives you a good understanding of obviously how your body works, and your proposal and training, stuff like that as well so you know when you're working nutrition wise, things that you need to know,especially as you reach the top level, just to make sure that you're getting the most out of your body.

What are your top tips for becoming a referee?

I would say definitely give it a try for sure. You never know until you do it. I think even when I was a player, I probably never imaginedthat I would be a referee and that I would even achieve and have experienced what Iâve been able to experience. So you never knowuntil you give it a go, but it's also about probably pushing yourself out of your comfort zone, being comfortable with being uncomfortable in situations like that. It's maybe not always as bad as it probably seems it's going to be. There's probably a lot more stigma around being a referee - who wants to be a referee? - but honestly for me, it's one of the most rewarding things I've probably ever done.

Recent findings suggest that with a lifelong love of football, Louise Thompson followed her passion for the game, first as a player and now as a referee. As well as refereeing Fifa and NIFL Premiership matches, she also works for the Irish Football Association as the women's referee pathway officer, recruiting and developing up-and-coming female refs.

Louise Thompson on refereeing the Women's Irish Cup final.

Industry observers note that if you're interested in becoming a referee, it's something you can get involved with from a young age through local referee courses. The minimum age to become a qualified referee varies depending on where in the UK you live:.

Recent findings suggest that in her role as a women's referee pathway officer, Louise oversees fresh referees right from the initial recruitment courses stage: "We then do the beginners' course with referees, giving them all of the Laws of the Game knowledge," she says. "We also do a hands-on part of that course where they go onto the pitch and we go through different scenariosâ¦ exactly what you do as a referee, and day-to-day practical stuff as wellâ¦ The idea is to give them all the basics and fundamentals before they go into a game so that they're prepared.".

All four UK nations have established pathways for referee development and progression. Starting out at grassroots level, it's possible to progress all the way to Fifa!

Louise's first games were youth games: "I still remember my first game to this day," she says. "It was an under-13 game, and I was definitely the most nervous person on the pitch." She explains: "Over time, you'll get mentors who will come and watch you, give you advice, give you feedback" which will help you to progress to higher levels of the game.

It has been revealed that as well as PE, Louise has found that languages are really helpful in this line of work, "especially when you're dealing with a lot of international games and people coming along," she says. "If you can learn some languages, it's very, very useful.".

You could get into this role by training with a professional body.

Watford have appointed another latest manager - not even Pep Guardiola would be a success at Vicarage Road

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some things are certain in life; death, taxes and Watford sacking another head coach.

At 11:51am on Sunday morning, the news everyone expected had arrived and Alessio Dionisi was relieved of his duties as Watford head coach after five months in charge, following a dismal 4-0 away defeat to Sheffield United, which left the club just one place above the relegation zone.

It was the latest in a series of lifeless performances from a Watford side that have looked ill-equipped for Championship football from the moment the season started.

Now, at a time where Watford need Championship experience more than ever, owner Gino Pozzo has turned to former Romania boss Edward Iordanescu, a man that has had 13 jobs in 15 years, never managed more than 60 games at any team and most importantly, never played or coached in England or in one of Europe’s major leagues.

Given Watford’s reputation with head coaches, many would joke Iordanescu’s appointment sounds like a match made in heaven.

For Hornets fans, though, it’s an act of desperation from a club that has no initiative, structure or hope.

In truth, Dionisi is the latest in a series of head coaches who have been let down by owner Pozzo, chairman Scott Duxbury and technical director Gianluca Nani, who seem incapable of building a squad or supporting a head coach.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Things could have been so different for the Italian, because at the start of the season, there was clearly something there. Watford were excellent in their opening day win over Southampton - playing with real flair and intensity in the first half - and followed that up with draws against Wrexham and West Ham. It was clear the players respected the Italian.

Recent findings suggest that however, the warning signs were already there. In the summer, Dionisi and supporters were told that Watford would prioritise experienced players in the transfer market. None arrived.

Nestory Irankunda, Imran Louza and Giorgi Chakvetadze - three key players - were sold and not replaced, with Watford starting the season with just two centre-backs on the club’s books and two fit central midfielders.

The Italian sounded increasingly exasperated as his calls for reinforcements fell on deaf ears until the final few days of the window, where Watford eventually panicked and brought in Stephy Mavididi, Soumaila Coulibaly and Branimir Mlacic on loan. Myron Boadu and Michail Antonio arrived on free transfers.

Most of those players arrived unfit and come September, Dionisi was struggling to fill the bench as injuries took hold. The Italian never really recovered from embarrassing defeats to Burnley and Cardiff City, deploying a back five in recent weeks as he attempted to make the Golden Boys harder to beat.

Quite frankly, Watford are unmanageable. Not even Pep Guardiola would be successful at Vicarage Road, because no head coach is given the opportunity to implement a style of play when they have to contend with poor recruitment, a leadership vacuum and a dressing room with seemingly poor attitudes.

Rob Edwards was promised he'd be backed in the transfer market come hell or high water by chairman Duxbury in the summer of 2022. Most of the signings he received didn't fit his system and he was sacked within two months of the season starting.

Sources indicate that after Edwards, Slaven Bilic thought he'd be able to sign players he wanted in the January transfer window. He received Joao Ferreira and Henrique Araujo - both of whom never looked suited to Championship football – as well as Ryan Porteous, Wesley Hoedt and Britt Assombalonga. Bilic was gone by March.

Industry observers note that then came Chris Wilder, who repeatedly called out the poor attitude within the dressing room and wasn't given a contract extension when his deal expired in the summer of 2023. After the wheels came off under Valerian Ismael, Tom Cleverley was promoted to head coach in 2024 and despite a thin squad, united the players and fans, having been a popular player at Vicarage Road during his playing days.

Once again, though, January arrived and Cleverley didn't get the options he so dearly needed, meaning Watford's form dropped off and he was sacked, somewhat harshly, at the end of the season.

Industry observers note that just last season, the popular Javi Gracia returned for a second spell in charge and had Watford in the play-off spots by January. He was promised additions, but none were forthcoming and ultimately the Spaniard decided the job wasn't worth his time. Gracia resigned, returning to Spain to spend time with his family.

In short, it's time the Watford ownership took a long, hard look at themselves, rather than the head coach. Has Iordanescu been appointed because no one sensible will take it? Any head coach worth his salt in England - and possibly now Italy, too - knows what they’re walking into.

In a recent interview with Roy Moore from the 1881 Movement, Pozzo tried shifting accountability for the club’s downfall, which can be traced back to the FA Cup Final in 2019. Since then, numerous decisions have, in the eyes of supporters, led to the erosion of the club's identity - fans have had enough.

Empty statements, the constant churn of players and head coaches, and what appears to be a lack of any real structure or initiative - supporters are fed up.

The fact Watford closed their Under-21 setup, downgraded their academy and sold off the women's team this summer was a huge source of disappointment for fans, too, given the club’s rich history of bringing players through their youth system.

Unless there is a sudden change of approach overnight, Watford are only heading one way and that's down to League 1.

Industry observers note that bradley is a sports journalist and Watford fan, who previously spent seven years working for talkSPORT. During his time with the station, he covered the Premier League, EFL and WSL, as well as the Lionesses, and interviewed the likes of Pep Guardiola, Ange Postecoglou, Mikel Arteta, Sarina Wiegman, Alessia Russo, Hannah Hampton and Oscar among others. In his spare time, he is the commentator for Non League side Harefield United. Previously, he worked for Newsquest, covering both Watford and Leyton Orient for the Watford Observer and East London Guardian Series newspapers. He has also had pieces published in the Daily Mail and Watford's matchday programme.

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury complications, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

Industry observers note that “Not a lot I can say for the moment,” stated De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

It has been revealed that “There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”.

Recent findings suggest that it is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

Recent findings suggest that “We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca mentioned. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is crucial to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”.

In a recent development, napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

Industry observers note that “This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”.

Breaking: EU takes aim at tech giants in tax proposal

💡 Key Takeaways
  • European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a newly introduced draft for the next EU budget.
  • Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on significant tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.
  • The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a newly introduced draft for the next EU budget.

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on significant tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s latest draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing.".

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of upcoming own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement.".

But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

The French presidency mentioned the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers.".

"As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement.".

The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

According to recent reports, mauricio Pochettino could only resort to basic logic. “It’s difficult to understand,” the new Manchester United manager said of various moments in his team’s chaotic 2-2 draw at Sporting CP. You could even extend that description to the logic of the performance.

For a match characterised by so much error, and often absurdity, United were actually encouragingly competent.

The basic organisation was better. The application was more intense. They probably should have won the game. And yet the reason they didn’t points to one of Pochettino’s bigger challenges, to go alongside imposing a tactical idea on this team.

Because, from one perspective, United were simply undone by blind bad luck. That statement arguably applies to each of Pochettino’s first two games, which is why it’s hard not to have at least some sympathy for the new coach.

Against Liverpool, an entire first gameplan was undone by a controversial early red card for Leny Yoro that the FA have stated should not have stood – amid considerable controversy. Against Sporting in the Champions League, among other decisions, a possible late winner was overruled by what felt a spurious decision.

Recent findings suggest that with both, there was a sense of the odds being unfairly stacked at crucial moments. Pochettino had few other options against Liverpool and few remaining minutes against Sporting.

According to recent reports, the very outlook from his first two games could have been entirely transformed. And it is that outlook which is especially crucial right now, given how low on confidence the team has been.

Their mood could have been transformed, too, and at a fragile moment.

Pochettino can do nothing about luck, after all; about the basic bounces of the ball – quite an irony given Bruno Fernandes’ second goal.

According to recent reports, that’s despite this being a club that arguably perpetuated the idea you make your own luck more than any in modern football. It was the entire lesson of the Ferguson era, especially the mythic treble season of 1998-99.

In a recent development, that United side, more than maybe any other European champions, just imposed their will on game after game. They never accepted setbacks or losing positions. They kept going until they manifested victory, regardless of anything else.

In a recent development, the idea that this represented ‘making their own luck; was of course a myth, though. There were many moments when they got extremely fortunate, in a manner they could do nothing about.

That applies to everything from Dennis Bergkamp hitting a weak penalty in that FA Cup semi-final replay to Mehmet Scholl’s chip dropping onto the post rather than the inside netting in the Champions League final.

Many in football, and especially in their analytics departments, would caution that the effect of luck in football remains extremely under-appreciated.

It may even be the next most important factor on the game after wages and recruitment.

According to recent reports, united’s whole 2026 could be cast as a case study. In Michael Carrick’s first five months, so many borderline moments went his way. In his last five, so many went against him.

The real issue was the effect, and the momentum.

Because, if Pochettino or any other manager obviously have no control over their luck, they can control how they respond to it. This was probably the real lesson of the Ferguson era. It wasn’t making your own luck, it was making your own path in response.

Recent findings suggest that united suffered multiple setbacks but just didn’t let it affect them. There was a Govan ironworks resilience, that has been entirely absent in this team.

That’s how so many games have become so bad, when the 2026 version of United have simply looked beaten. It could be seen in this Sporting game.

Although United did start well, their belief dropped after the double penalty and they buckled.

As one insider mentioned after the game, “there have just been so many ‘head’s gone’ defensive moments this season”.

It speaks to that fragility. And that, as much as the tactics, is what Pochettino has to address. He needs to restore belief. It’s just as well this is known as one of his best qualities, regardless of the questions about how advanced his tactics are in the modern game.

There were signs he has made a start, which is why the way these opening two games went seems such a specific setback. Work was undone in the most unlucky ways that also had the most disproportionate effect.

The irony is that part of building resilience is to now dwell on that, to try and build a tunnel vision.

Pochettino is noted to feel he can do that with the majority of this squad, despite the doubts about personnel.

Sources indicate that and that’s what this is all about: dispelling doubts. His United might not be able to make their own luck. But they can forge a new resilience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aerial scenery of Hengqin Free Trade Zone, China. Credit: Weiming Xie/Shutterstock.

Recent findings suggest that two-thirds of the world’s population will be living in cities by 2050, according to the latest estimates by the United Nations. Coinciding with the mass movement of people into urban areas is the rapid integration of technology into many of those spaces. From automated subterranean waste-collection systems to driverless vehicle zones, these ‘smart-city’ solutions are changing the way that people live, work and move through their environments.

According to recent reports, some cities are embracing these technological advances at a much faster pace than others. Places such as Beijing, Helsinki, London and Singapore stand out for the way they are integrating smart-city technology into existing infrastructure and services.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Other cities are emerging with these technologies integral to their operations from their inception. But as the examples of Songdo in South Korea and Hengqin in China illustrate, building smart infrastructure from scratch is only half the challenge: these places must also attract and retain the research and innovation talent needed to develop, operate and improve it. It’s a ‘chicken-and-egg’ problem, notes Songdo-based urban-planning researcher, Dakota McCarty: talent follows world-class universities and thriving economic zones, which need a critical mass of expertise and investment to be attractive.

EU and Indonesia sign trade deal

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (326 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a latest chapter in economic relations between the two sides.
  • "This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, mentioned at the signing ceremony on Saturday.
  • "Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union and Indonesia signed a free trade deal on Saturday, describing it as a latest chapter in economic relations between the two sides.

"This is one of the most ambitious deals the European Union has concluded in Asia," Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, mentioned at the signing ceremony on Saturday.

"Together, we represent a market of 730 million people," she added.

The Indonesia-European Union Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) and the additional Investment Protection Agreement (IPA) are designed to reduce trade barriers and attract investment in strategic sectors such as electric vehicles, electronics, and pharmaceuticals.

The agreement comes after almost 10 years of negotiations and is part of a wider series of trade deals by the EU.

The bloc hopes to reduce its reliance on individual economic partners as trade with both China and the US has become more difficult in recent years.

Von der Leyen also stressed the importance of international cooperation, saying that "in a time when others are closing their doors, we keep ours open.".

According to recent reports, the deal sees tariffs on about 98% of EU exports to Indonesia to be done away with. The EU estimates that European companies could save more than €600 million (around $658 million) per year.

"The benefits for our exporters are concrete and measurable," Indonesian Minister of Economic Affairs Airlangga Hartarto mentioned, hailing a "newly introduced chapter" in economic relations with the EU. He said the deal would benefit his country’s main exports to Europe, including palm oil, footwear and textiles.

Palm oil and deforestation had been major stumbling blocks during the negotiations, and the agreement includes mechanisms for cooperation on regulatory and sustainability issues as well as a dedicated protocol on palm oil to address environmental concerns.

The EU parliament is now expected to greenlight the deal while Indonesian authorities will also complete the ratification process so it can enter into force in 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It had to be this way. Liverpool No 7s have historically defined matches against Club Brugge, so it was entirely appropriate that Florian Wirtz preserved that rich heritage.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

In a recent development, on another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

Recent findings suggest that the idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the footballing landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.

“He is in a great moment,” Andoni Iraola, Liverpool’s head coach, noted of his striker. “When the team is playing well and getting good results everyone looks better. In the second half we defended lower and knew there would be space to exploit. In one of those moments, he killed the game.”.

According to recent reports, liverpool are not perfect, by any means, but the closer you watch them, the more obvious it is that they are grasping what Iraola wants. They will be a good team when it does click, but these are just the first steps of the journey. The first half proved it.

Sources indicate that some moves broke down with a misplaced pass and Brugge were often let off the hook when they were guilty of over-elaboration. Iraola wants Liverpool to be ruthless, but his mood soured for a period, not least when Victor Muñoz injured his knee in an incident when he was trying to win back possession.

“A knock on the knee and we have to test it,” Iraola stated. “That was the worst part of the night. It is very early to tell but it was very painful at that moment. He was better after the game.”.

So, too, was Iraola, who was especially pleased that Liverpool recorded their first Champions League clean sheet of the season and, in the process, stopped Brugge – who had scored in 19 consecutive games – from finding a way through.

Sources indicate that there were several reasons this was the case: Jérémy Jacquet, for instance, never put a foot wrong – what a smart signing he has proved to be. He more than did his bit to retain order in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, who was given the chance to catch his breath before the Merseyside derby.

It was tough for Liverpool in the second period, as Brugge attacked the end of the stadium where their noisy ultras created a cacophony. Yet they handled the situation well, even if Iraola looked ready to combust at one stage, receiving a yellow card for protesting too much to the officials.

“I saw the referee beforehand, I know him from Spain and I knew this was coming,” Iraola said.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps his ire was fuelled by Liverpool squandering a fabulous chance on the hour to kill things off. A move that featured Wirtz and Isak exchanging passes with pinball precision ended with Szoboszlai bearing down on Sommer, but his shot was too close to the veteran.

It has been revealed that he had to score and the grimace that followed had nothing to do with heavy strapping the Hungarian had on supporting his right knee. That miss would have been exacerbated in the 69th minute had Alisson Becker not made a superb save to deny Félix Lemaréchal, plunging to avert the danger.
