Tech Report: Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1030 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.
  • In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner.
  • According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.

In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.

Recent findings suggest that as a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.

To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.

Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.

Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18.

Recent findings suggest that beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current aims would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.

Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.

Sources indicate that parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.

Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.

"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.

"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he mentioned.

The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.

It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens.".

The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.

Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.

Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.

But Germany's proposal differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.

The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.

"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them.".

Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.

It has been revealed that "If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions.".

In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.

Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.

Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.

"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he remarked.

Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.

Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, states the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.

"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.

The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains.
  • In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV.
  • Recent findings suggest that although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the latest HIV-vaccine strategies aim to trigger the development of antibodies that can prevent infection by a range of HIV strains. Credit: 3DMedisphere/SPL.

In the mid-2000s, a young woman in the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa became infected with HIV. Her story could have represented just another sobering statistic in the epidemic that was tearing through the region, but instead, she became a source of inspiration for scientists and of hope for millions. Enrolled in a study to track the course of newly acquired infections, the woman mounted a ferocious immune response to the virus over the next several years as doctors in the study treated her and took regular blood samples to monitor what was going on in her body.

Recent findings suggest that although she could not control the virus without the help of drugs, the antibodies she raised against HIV are recognized as among the strongest that have ever been discovered1. The woman is known in the literature as CAP256.

According to recent reports, scientists now think that by mimicking some of the key elements of an infection like hers, they might be able to train other people’s immune systems to make similarly potent antibodies that can block a diverse array of HIV strains. Ultimately, they say, they might achieve one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine that can stop HIV in its tracks.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it.

It has been revealed that “We have a line of sight to an efficacious vaccine,” says Mark Feinberg, president and chief executive of the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative (IAVI) in Latest York City. “The scientific promise is greater than it’s ever been.”.

Recent findings suggest that this year, several teams described vaccination strategies that — in monkeys — can trigger the production of what are known as broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs), molecules that can completely shut down an infection from a diverse range of HIV strains before it begins2–4. “No one has achieved that before. It’s a very important milestone,” claims Rogier Sanders, a virologist at Amsterdam University Medical Centre.

Humans who have received components of similar vaccines can produce precursors to these bnAbs5–7, suggesting that with further refinement, an effective vaccine is possible.

Success is by no means guaranteed, notes Feinberg. HIV has proved a formidable foe for vaccine developers in the past. And there is another factor that adds complications. The availability of successful drugs, such as lenacapavir, that prevent HIV infection might make it difficult to test how well a vaccine works. Meanwhile, devastating cuts to the US funding that supported preclinical and clinical research for HIV have left some efforts on a precipice.

“We’re in a better position than we’ve ever been, and just at this time, we’ve seen the funding streams cut off,” notes Dennis Burton, an immunologist and virologist at Scripps Research, a research institute in La Jolla, California.

It has been revealed that the latest glimmers of success follow decades of failure. Initially, scientists looking to develop an HIV vaccine followed a strategy that had been successful for many other viruses, including hepatitis B: administer a lab-made version of the proteins that viruses use to attach to host cells and the body should start producing antibodies that will block infection. In HIV’s case, it’s the surface protein known as envelope that latches onto a molecular receptor on human T cells so that the virus can infect them. “There was only one protein, and so it seemed straightforward,” claims Sallie Permar, a vaccinologist and paediatrician at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York City.

Sources indicate that starting in the 1980s, researchers made vaccines that contained the HIV envelope protein, to elicit antibodies against it, but the vaccines failed to prevent infection in clinical-trial participants. HIV mutates rapidly and most circulating strains were still able to mount an infection. “With HIV, there are millions of strains circulating simultaneously. Taking out one does nothing,” states Richard Wyatt, a viral immunologist at Scripps Research.

Recent findings suggest that trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Industry observers note that researchers tried other strategies, such as vaccines that recruited ‘killer’ T cells to wipe out infected cells, and those that delivered a wider diversity of proteins to overcome HIV’s penchant for mutation. In 2009, a clinical trial in Thailand reported modest signs of protection for a vaccine that triggered both T-cell and antibody responses8. But efforts to replicate those results failed, and that strategy was abandoned, too.

It has been revealed that one overarching problem, states Feinberg, was that nobody knew what the immunological signature — the measurable biological response after injection — of an effective HIV vaccine looked like, so the only way to assess a candidate was to conduct large-scale efficacy trials and hope for the best. “It was all a shot in the dark,” says Burton.

Recent findings suggest that that attitude began to change after the discovery of bnAbs. In the 1990s, teams led by Burton and microbiologist Hermann Katinger, then at the University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences in Vienna, identified the first of them in individuals who were living with HIV9,10. These bnAbs could protect monkeys from infection by HIV strains circulating in Europe and America, but it took large doses, which were unlikely to be reached and sustained with a vaccine. And the protection was less effective against some strains from Africa.

In the 2000s, Burton’s team developed a way to sort through vast numbers of B cells — the immune cells that produce antibodies — for the rare ones that make bnAbs. After screening around 1,800 people living with HIV, they identified a pair of highly potent bnAbs, made by a donor in Africa, that blocked infection from dozens of HIV strains11. “That ignited the field,” notes Burton.

Researchers would have to learn how to train the immune system to produce these kinds of bnAb. The strategies to do so emerged from the recognition that bnAbs often develop gradually in HIV-infected individuals such as CAP256. It happens through a sustained “cat and mouse game” between the fast-changing virus and an immune system struggling to keep up, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Diseases and the University of Witwatersrand, both in Johannesburg, who analysed CAP256’s blood.

It has been revealed that to mimic that struggle in an uninfected person, researchers first deliver a ‘priming’ immunogen — a portion or complete copy of HIV’s envelope. This shot awakens B cells, triggering them to divide and become active. Subsequent doses deliver distinct versions of the HIV envelope to first ‘shape’ and then ‘polish’ the antibodies produced. The goal is to guide the awakened B cells through a process called affinity maturation, in which the antibodies develop extensive mutations that improve their binding and breadth. The key is that the most capable B cells are recruited early and the antibodies that they produce are honed over time (see ‘Targeted vaccines’).

In a recent development, source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

Recent findings suggest that sanders says that this strategy, sometimes known as germline targeting, is a bit like looking for an elite footballer among pools of youth players. Rather than trying to train everyone up to an expert level, they want to identify talent early and nurture it to superstardom. “We’re scouting the talented B cells,” Sanders says.

Researchers have taken different approaches to scouting these cells. After Moore and colleagues discovered CAP256’s antibodies, they sequenced the viruses circulating in her blood to identify what might have triggered and shaped the antibodies’ production.

A modified version of the envelope protein from one such virus has shown promise as a priming agent for the immune system in monkeys and is now being trialled in humans, states virologist George Shaw who co-led the preclinical work for this2 with virologist Beatrice Hahn, both at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.

Another team, led by William Schief at Scripps Research, used computational structural modelling and cell studies to design immunogens that activate a specific subset of B cells that make antibodies capable of blocking the binding site through which HIV latches onto T cells5.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

Trump team guts AIDS-eradication programme and slashes HIV research grants.

According to recent reports, in small trials of vaccination with either protein or mRNA-based versions of this immunogen12, which is called eOD-GT8, nearly all participants developed ‘bnAb precursors’. These are antibodies with the desired genetic and structural characteristics of a bnAb that blocks the T-cell binding site on the envelope protein, but not the bevy of mutations that makes bnAbs elite. In participants who also got a booster shot of a different immunogen, the antibodies picked up mutations that improved their binding and neutralization abilities. “It worked beautifully,” claims Schief, who is also vice-president for protein design at Moderna Therapeutics in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

#129171. Breaking: X is giving creators more reasons to post vertical videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (719 w)

Breaking: X is giving creators more reasons to post vertical videos

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A short video can make it from TikTok to Instagram Reels to the group chat before lunch.
  • Industry observers note that on Wednesday, Nov.
  • X claims video is already its fastest-growing format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A short video can make it from TikTok to Instagram Reels to the group chat before lunch. X wants more of those clips to land in its feed, too, and it's giving some creators a reason to post videos they've already made.

Industry observers note that on Wednesday, Nov. 25, X laid out its aims to get more creators making, sharing, and earning money from videos on the platform. It revealed off an upgraded editor that lets creators record, crop, and caption videos without leaving X, confirmed that its clipping tool is now available on the web, and highlighted an invite-only bonus it's been testing since October for creators who regularly post short, vertical videos.

X claims video is already its fastest-growing format. "Posts with video get 5x the reach and engagement, and 36% of all impressions now go to video," the organization’s creator team wrote on Nov. 20.

Sources indicate that the editor lets creators record in segments, use a green screen, or turn horizontal footage into a vertical clip with one tap. They can also trim the footage, generate captions, add text, and pick a thumbnail before posting. A separate patch, announced Nov. 20, lets creators mix up to 20 photos and videos in a single swipeable post. Those tools join React with Video, which X introduced over the summer to let people respond on camera with the original post behind them.

Recent findings suggest that X is also paying some creators to try vertical video through its Video Kickstart Bonus, an invite-only pilot it began testing in October. To earn the bonus, creators must post 15 qualifying videos on 15 different days within about a month. Each video must be their own work, in a vertical 9:16 format, and under three minutes. A TikTok, Reel, or YouTube Short can count as long as it’s free of another platform’s branding. Creators can see their bonus amount in Creator Studio, X's dashboard for creator tools and payouts. Participants who don’t already have Premium+ also get a free year.

Original Content Rewards also gives creators a way to earn when someone else shares a moment from their video. X's clipping tool, now available on the web as well as iOS and Android, lets customers pull an excerpt, add their take, and post it with a link back to the original. Both the person who made the video and the person who posted the clip can earn if they're enrolled in the program.

As X creator product lead Allegra Jacchia put it Wednesday, the goal is to make sure that "when someone clips their video, they get the credit and a share of the earnings.".

Sources indicate that X first rolled out clipping on iOS and Android earlier this month, and Wednesday's announcement confirmed it’s now available on the web, too. To make a clip, open the repost menu on an eligible prerecorded video and select "Clip video." From there, you can trim the footage to between five and 60 seconds and add your commentary before posting. The original video must run for at least two minutes, and the clip can take up no more than 30 percent of it. (So if you're clipping a two-minute video, you get up to 36 seconds.).

Industry observers note that the clip plays right in the feed. For everyone in the replies asking for the full video, there's a shortcut. Tap the "Clip from" label and X takes you straight to the moment in the original video where the excerpt starts. Russo grew up in Maidstone, Kent and football always featured in her life.

Industry observers note that “Football has always been a massive part of my life,” she remarked. “Growing up, my dad would take me to watch women’s games at Charlton, and I remember looking up to those players and dreaming of doing the same one day.

“To see how far the game has come is incredible. Women’s football is now about so much more than what happens on the pitch. It’s influencing fashion, culture and bringing communities together in ways I could never have imagined growing up.

Now one of the leading strikers in world football, Russo believes her calm approach is one of her biggest strengths when it comes to finding the back of the net.

According to recent reports, "I've always been really laid back. I'm always wanting to win. Just because I'm not angry or shouting or screaming, doesn't mean I don't want to win and I don't want to score," she stated.

"I think that calmness is something that I try and bring to the game. And I think as a striker, you have to be calm in and around the box. When things aren't going your way, I just kind of strip it back. I like to train hard and then whatever happens in the game happens.

Industry observers note that "You can't control a whole lot as a No.9. You're quite reliant on other players. But what you can control is the moments that you do get.".

One of football's most-hyped 16-year-olds - what next for JJ Gabriel?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.
  • It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.
  • Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

JJ Gabriel featured for Manchester United's senior team in pre-season.

It has been one of the biggest transfer sagas of the year - around a player who has never played competitive football.

Forward JJ Gabriel, who has recently turned 16, walked out on Manchester United in September and now has a verbal agreement to join Real Madrid.

Before even playing a senior game - barring friendlies - he has told Spanish newspaper Marca his "dream is to win the Ballon d'Or".

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - with Cypriot and Irish lineage - but he changed his name, reportedly for commercial purposes.

His father, London-born Joe O'Cearuill, played twice for the Republic of Ireland - but the highest level he played at club level was a loan spell with Brighton in League One and one minute in the Uefa Cup with St Patrick's Athletic. He has been actively involved in his son's career.

Gabriel was scheduled to become Manchester United's youngest ever player in the Carabao Cup against Brighton on 16 September, but had told the club he planned to leave by then.

How long will Gabriel have to wait for a first-team debut now? In the past 10 years Real have only handed two debuts to 17-year-olds and none to a 16-year-old.

When Real boss Jose Mourinho was asked about Gabriel on Friday, he said: "I don't have a feeling [about Gabriel]. I don't have a feeling with players who don't work with me.".

In fact, Real have not even announced anything yet - despite Gabriel posting a 50-second video montage on social media saying goodbye to United this week.

Madrid-bound Gabriel posts farewell Man Utd message.

Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market.

For a while now Madrid have been getting the best young talents early and turning them into Galacticos before they cost in excess of 100m euros.

Vinicius Junior and Rodrygo came that way, then Endrick - and Gabriel is seen as the next.

It fits the policy run by Jose Angel Sanchez, the director general, and Juni Calafat, head of scouting. It is a long-term bet on one of the most promising young players in the international game.

Barcelona looked at him too, and backed away because the commissions were too high. Madrid believe in the player so much that they were willing to pay whatever it took to get the deal done.

The expectations are very high and the aim is for him to reach the first team. They want him at Castilla - Real's reserve team - but the situation right now does not allow it.

Castilla and Real Madrid C cannot sign players until January, so for the time being he is expected to play for the Juvenil - the under-18s.

Recent findings suggest that madrid also learned from the Martin Odegaard period that training with the first team while playing for the B side is a bad idea. So the proposal is a spell in the B side, and when he is ready, Gabriel jumps straight into the first team.

According to recent reports, where Madrid are less happy is with how things have unfolded. Madrid wanted to set the timing themselves and be discreet, because they do not want problems with Manchester United and do not want to upset anyone. At Real Madrid, nobody is bigger than the club.

In a recent development, the idea was to keep everything quiet until January and announce it then. But with Gabriel already training in Madrid, the secret was never going to last.

Who is Gabriel's upcoming agent, Ali Barat?

"Players are moving to him because his reputation is that he'll get you a move to a bigger club," one Premier League club source told BBC Sport.

Dubai-based Barat does not just consider himself a super-agent, but a "boutique" super-agent.

Born in Iran and raised in London, Barat claims he fell into football almost by accident after many years in international business.

After initially working as an intermediary at low-level clubs, he founded Epic Sports in January 2020.

According to recent reports, his major football experience before that? The football game Championship Manager.

According to recent reports, "I was always trading players," he told ESPN this year. "I was obsessed with every single player around the world.".

This was not just about living out a fantasy in the real world. Barat was drawn into the profession because of the vast sums agents can earn in commission.

Sources indicate that what makes his agency "boutique"? Unlike the top operations which have a huge number of players on their books, Epic Sports aims to have just 22 - two for each position.

This, Barat argues, ensures there is never any conflict of interest in how he represents his players.

Barat offers bespoke management of a player's career and came to prominence in the summer of 2025 when 15 of his players moved on.

This included Dean Huijsen joining Real Madrid, Nicolas Jackson moving to Bayern Munich and Xavi Simons signing for Tottenham Hotspur. Noni Madueke left Chelsea for Arsenal, and the Gunners signed Piero Hincapie.

This led to Barat being named Golden Boy Best Agent for the second time in three years.

Yet he is largely the figurehead, with agents working on his behalf around Europe. For instance, Epic has three other agents registered with the English Football Association (FA).

Barat, who also brokered Moises Caicedo's move to Chelsea, says he uses social media, and in particular influencer Fabrizio Romano, to amplify stories and agree transfers on his terms.

He is an unashamed self-publicist, too.

"Ali Barat redefines the game again," read an Epic Sports press release to announce Jackson's loan move to Bayern. No other agency seems to promote itself in this way.

The largely AI-generated video which confirmed Gabriel had joined Epic Sports was right on brand.

Gabriel's deal is part of a latest venture: Epic Future - and this presents an ethical problem.

It has been revealed that "It is about targeting the biggest young players, especially where they're not necessarily on the longest contracts," a Premier League source said. "And move them overseas for cheap fees.

"The original club will get a few 100,000 euros if that, and everyone else will hoover up millions and millions and millions - including his family.".

Transferring a player to Europe also opens the door to future sell-on fees for an agent, which is against FA regulations.

It is this new focus on younger players which has started to cause friction at some top clubs.

No club wants to lose players they have spent years developing for nothing, only for an agent to reap the rewards.

Manchester United had to work hard 18 months ago to convince JJ Gabriel and his family that Old Trafford was the right place to further his football education.

The major question is, did they overpromise in doing so?

Sources close to the player eventually felt they were let down and United did not deliver on what was expected.

Certainly around Gabriel's pre-season minutes and presence in the squad for the Champions League opener against Azerbaijan title winners Sabah FK, which it was felt would be a perfect opportunity for the youngster to make his debut.

Industry observers note that by the time the Carabao Cup tie against Brighton came round, there was no faith Gabriel would be brought on. Given United lost 3-2, there is merit in that stance.

The secondary elements are where will Gabriel develop the most?

United's academy is one of the best in England at producing young players, but given his size, will the forward benefit more from being in a less physical environment?

There has been a lot of sniping around his decision to leave United, but his stats are impressive and he is clearly a player of huge potential. United would certainly have wished the situation had not unfolded the way it has.

#129163. Breaking: Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)

Breaking: Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system.
  • Sources indicate that "We were actually looking for planets," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement.
  • According to recent reports, so surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system.

Sources indicate that "We were actually looking for planets," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement. "Instead, we found something much more surprising.".

According to recent reports, so surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years. Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here.".

This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects.

Industry observers note that A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity. This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across.

Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass.

Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as promptly.

In a recent development, one of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual.

SPIRou discovers planets by measuring how much their gravity tugs on their host star. Think of a star and planet orbiting a kind of gravitational balancing point between them called a center of mass. This center of mass is usually inside the star, since the star is far more massive than the planet, but crucially not at its very center, so the star appears to wobble to and fro around the combined center of mass.

Recent findings suggest that the spectrometer measures this wobble in the form of a Doppler shift in the star's light that can be translated into the velocity at which the star is moving around this center of mass. Astronomers call this a 'radial velocity'. A large gas giant like Jupiter might incur a radial velocity of hundreds of meters per second, while an Earth-mass planet generates a radial velocity of tens of meters.

Industry observers note that yet the object that SPIRou found orbiting close to the red dwarf was creating a huge radial velocity signals of 10 miles (16 kilometers) per second. Whatever it was, it was not a planet. With the help of the eight-meter Gemini North telescope on Hawaii's Mauna Kea, Artigau's team were able to identify the mystery object as a white dwarf.

"The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star," said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and a co-author of the study.

Sources indicate that white dwarfs are not exactly rare, and even finding two white dwarfs together is not unheard of: WD 0727+482 is a binary white dwarf system 37 light-years away, for example. To encounter two white dwarfs in a triple system with a regular star though is a precious find.

The reason being that the masses of white dwarfs are not generally well defined. Yet their masses are not random; they are directly connected to the mass of the star that produced them.

Sources indicate that thanks to the newly discovered white dwarf being separated from the red dwarf by about 4.6 astronomical units (688 million kilometers/428 million miles) – that's closer than Jupiter orbits our sun – Artigau's team were able to measure their masses to within an uncertainty of less than 1%. They found that the red dwarf has a mass 42% that of our sun and the newly discovered white dwarf has a mass 62% that of our sun. When the white dwarf was a regular star it would have had a mass 40% greater than our sun. The second more distant white dwarf orbits the pair of them.

The Welopō'ai system is therefore a good system for testing our models of stellar evolution that dictate how massive a white dwarf should be. If we know the white dwarf's mass with high precision, scientists can also use that as a starting point from which to explore the extreme physics of the white dwarf's condensed matter, which is being held up and prevented from contracting any further by something called electron degeneracy pressure – the unwillingness of negatively charged electrons to crush down any further and merge with positively charged protons to form neutrons. That takes the extra gravity from a more massive star to form a neutron star.

Recent findings suggest that so why should Welopō'ai not exist? The trouble is that when stars turn into red giants they really stir things up. Even if the red giant didn't expand out as far as the red dwarf, the expansion should have destabilized the red dwarf's orbit and potentially even caused it to crash into the red giant. Yet here the red dwarf is in a happily stable orbit like nothing had happened.

According to recent reports, "That is the question driving our next observations," said Dufour. It is hoped that further, more detailed, measurements of the gravitational interactions between the three members of the Welopō'ai system will help the team disentangle the evolutionary history of the trio to better understand their orbits and how the red dwarf survived. And because they are so relatively close to us, we have the advantage of being able to make high-precision measurements.

"Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises," remarked Artigau. "Even when we're searching for planets, our universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.".

The discovery of the Welopō'ai triple system is described in a paper published on Nov. 19 in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Sources indicate that keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

  • It has been revealed that spaceX claims the factory it’s building in Bastrop, Texas, could start turning out satellites for launch as early as late 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an AI chatbot may be able to answer a question in seconds, but the chips doing the work need a steady supply of electricity and a way to get rid of all the heat they generate. SpaceX wants to put some of those chips on satellites and power them with sunlight. In outer space.

It has been revealed that on Wednesday, Nov. 25, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) gave Elon Musk's SpaceX conditional approval to deploy up to 1 million satellites for its Starmind project, a network of orbital data centers that would process information for use back on Earth. According to the FCC, it's "the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.".

It has been revealed that spaceX claims the factory it’s building in Bastrop, Texas, could start turning out satellites for launch as early as late 2027. The FCC's deadline for the first one is Nov. 25, 2033. By then, SpaceX has to have a Starmind satellite in its assigned orbit and running.

Recent findings suggest that two years later, the FCC expects 100,000 satellites to be operating. That's nearly nine times as many satellites as SpaceX's Starlink network has in orbit today. The next deadlines are 500,000 by Nov. 2038 and the full million by Nov. 2040. Under the terms of the order, missing those deadlines would void the authorization.

SpaceX is counting on its Starship rocket to carry the heavy satellites into orbit in large numbers. Amazon Leo, which is building a rival to Starlink, called the proposal a "lofty ambition rather than a real blueprint" in a March petition. Amazon argued it could take SpaceX centuries to put a million satellites in orbit. The FCC rejected Amazon's petition, along with separate challenges from Viasat and the American Astronomical Society.

In a recent development, spaceX wants the satellites themselves to do the computing. Each one would carry AI chips, solar panels to power them, and radiators to release the heat the chips generate. In some orbits, the panels could collect sunlight nearly around the clock. The satellites would use lasers to pass data between one another and send results back to Earth through Starlink.

According to recent reports, in August (pre-Jensen Huang drama), Nvidia remarked SpaceX plans to adapt its Vera Rubin computing system for the first generation of satellites, "bringing the first CPU built for AI agents to one of the world’s most ambitious AI deployments." (CPU stands for central processing unit.) The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

In a recent development, one of the questions for any data center in space is how well its chips will hold up over time. Google is testing that with Project Suncatcher, a prototype satellite that released on a SpaceX rocket in October. The chip has already run an AI model in orbit and sent back a haiku about being in space. ("Blue marble below, Data streams in silent grace, Starlight feeds my core.") Google is now testing how the hardware handles radiation and temperature swings.

The same sunlight that would power the satellites could also make them visible from the ground.

Recent findings suggest that the American Astronomical Society said its preliminary simulations suggest that, if SpaceX deploys the full million, tens of thousands could be visible to the naked eye around the world. Reflected sunlight could also leave bright streaks in telescope images and make faint objects harder to see. How much the sky actually changes would depend on details like the satellites' size, materials, and orbits.

Industry observers note that the FCC stated SpaceX's commitment to work with the National Science Foundation was enough to address the optical astronomy concerns raised in the proceeding. But Starlink has already left its mark on telescope images. At California's Zwicky Transient Facility, for example, researchers found Starlink streaks in 18 percent of images taken at twilight in Aug. 2021, up from less than half a percent in late 2019. A separate study published this year found that several newer Starlink designs were typically dimmer than the originals but still brighter than the goal SpaceX agreed to work toward.

Recent findings suggest that there's also the question of what happens when the satellites are done working. Under current FCC rules, satellites at those altitudes have to come back through Earth's atmosphere at the end of their missions. SpaceX asked for the option to move some retired satellites into other orbits, including around the sun. The FCC put that request on hold and notes SpaceX has to submit a final plan for limiting space debris before deploying any Starmind satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers (or about 373 miles).

Industry observers note that if Starmind reaches the scale SpaceX has in mind, getting satellites out of orbit safely will be as much a part of running the network as getting them up there. And the launch schedule alone is a tall order. Even if SpaceX gets half a million satellites running by Nov. 2038, it would have just two years to get another half million into orbit and operational. Luckily, that's not my job.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.
  • Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.
  • The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.

Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.

The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.

The winner of the award - newly introduced for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.

Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, noted: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate.

"Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game.

"It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner.".

The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.

The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).

Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

Sources indicate that sorry, this vote cannot be loaded. In order to vote you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

Meet the SPOTY Men's Footballer of the Year contenders.

Club: Real Madrid Position: Midfield.

Bellingham made history this summer as he became the first Englishman to score as many as seven goals at a major tournament.

In a superb World Cup for the midfielder, he memorably netted twice in back-to-back games to help the Three Lions beat Mexico and Norway.

That meant he joined exalted tech giant as the first player to score two or more goals in successive World Cup knockout games since Diego Maradona in 1986, and the second youngest in history behind Pele in 1958.

Bellingham also became the youngest European player to make an appearance at four different major tournaments, and also reached the milestone of 50 caps at a younger age than any other England men's player.

The goals continued to flow for Real Madrid, too, with Bellingham notching his 50th for the club to move above the legendary Zinedine Zidane in the Los Blancos' all-time scoring charts.

Bellingham was recently joined in the England squad by his brother Jobe.

Club: Bayern Munich Position: Forward.

In a stunning year of goalscoring, Kane become the first Englishman for 25 years (and only fifth in history) to win the Ballon d'Or - awarded to the world's best footballer.

His tally of 73 goals in 65 matches for club and country during a stellar 2025-26 season has only been surpassed in one of Europe's top five leagues by Lionel Messi's 82 for Barcelona and Argentina in 2011-12.

Kane scored 61 of those goals in just 51 appearances for Bayern Munich as he helped the Bavarians to a league and cup double. His total was 19 more than any other player in Europe's top five divisions.

Already England's record goalscorer, he surpassed Peter Shilton's mark of 125 appearances to become the most-capped Englishman in history.

Six goals at this summer's World Cup also helped him overtake Gary Lineker as the Three Lions' record scorer at the tournament, while he joined David Beckham as the only Englishmen to score in three separate World Cups.

Kane scored his first England goal 79 seconds into his debut in 2015.

Club: Real Madrid Position: Forward.

Mbappe came out on top of an enthralling tussle with Lionel Messi at the 2026 World Cup to become the leading goalscorer in the tournament's history.

The France forward, who is still only 27, took his tally to 22 from just three World Cups to finish one ahead of the great Argentine.

Mbappe's 10 goals from eight games this summer meant he won his second World Cup Golden Boot - a feat no player has managed before.

It also made him the first man to reach double figures at a World Cup since Gerd Muller in 1970, with only Just Fontaine (13) and Sandor Kocsis (11) having scored more goals in a single tournament.

Other achievements in a standout year included him finishing runner-up in the Ballon d'Or awards and overtaking Olivier Giroud as France's all-time leading goalscorer.

He scored 25 times to retain his title as La Liga's top scorer during a 2025-26 campaign in which he netted 42 goals in all competitions for Real Madrid.

Mbappe has won eight consecutive league golden boots.

Club: Barcelona Position: Midfield.

Midfield maestro Rodri earned yet another accolade in his incredible career when he was awarded the Golden Ball trophy for the World Cup's best player.

By captaining Spain to glory in the US, Rodri became only the fourth male player to win the World Cup, European Championship, Champions League and Ballon d'Or - following in the footsteps of legendary Germans Gerd Muller and Franz Beckenbauer and France's Zinedine Zidane.

His achievements were made all the more special given doubts remained over whether he would recapture his best form after a long recovery from a serious knee injury in 2024.

According to recent reports, then Manchester City boss Pep Guardiola predicted he would return to his best at the World Cup and he was right. Rodri completed 756 passes there - the most in the tournament since records began in 1966.

His final season at Manchester City before departing for Barcelona ended in familiar fashion with a domestic cup double taking his trophy haul with the club to 14.

Rodri scored the goal that won Manchester City the Champions League in 2023.

Club: Barcelona Position: Forward.

Lamine Yamal continues to rewrite the record books with his astonishing exploits for club and country.

Just days after his 19th birthday, the Spaniard became the youngest footballer to have played in - and won - both a World Cup and a European Championship. The only players younger than him to play in a World Cup final are Brazil's Pele in 1958 and Giuseppe Bergomi for Italy in 1982.

For the second year running, his performances led to a podium place at the Ballon d'Or and at the same award ceremony he became the first footballer in history to win the Young Talent of the Year three years in succession.

At club level, he was named La Liga's Best Player courtesy of a starring role in Barcelona's title success. The teenager ended the season with an impressive 24 goals and 18 assists across all competitions.

He recently broke Kylian Mbappe's record for the most goals by a teenager in Champions League history.

Lamine Yamal was 16 years and 362 days when he scored at the European Championship in 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pep Guardiola has been out of work since bringing an end to a decade at Manchester City this summer – and has suggested that his next job could be in charge of a national team.

Guardiola won six Premier League titles during his time at the Etihad, before deciding to step down at the end of last season.

In an interview this week though, the Catalan indicated that he sees his next step as being “a national team”, after talks to become Italy boss during the summer.

Guardiola opted not to take the Italy job, believing at the time that he needed a break from football, but has since been linked with the USA vacancy.

Mauricio Pochettino had been in charge of the American national team since 2024, leading them to the last 16 of this summer’s World Cup, but brought his tenure to an end last week to take charge of Manchester United.

Given that Guardiola is the highest profile manager currently out of work, and is one of the greatest of all time, having previously won two Champion Leagues and three La Liga titles with Barcelona, plus three Bundesliga titles with Bayern Munich, links to the job were inevitable.

Pochettino has said he would be in favour of Guardiola succeeding him as US boss, and former American national team goalkeeper Brad Friedel, who won 82 caps for his country, also admits it would be an intriguing appointment.

He warns though that even bringing in someone like Guardiola would not suddenly transform the national team into potential World Cup winners.

“I don’t know really what the discussions are within US soccer,” the 55-year-old told FFT, speaking in association with nye casino.

“We need the players to be able to win World Cups, and I think there's a lot to break down with that.

“Do I think Pep Guardiola is one of the best managers ever? Yes. Does that mean if you hire him that the US will win the World Cup? No. But it would be a little bit of a buzz.”.

Industry News: Can AI make Thanksgiving less painful?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I have a liberal friend who I was talking with the other day about looks for Thanksgiving.
  • "My uncle sits in a chair watching Fox News on his phone, and my great-aunt will try to tell me in so many ways, without telling me, that I’m going to hell for being gay.".
  • Recent findings suggest that every November, we all pretend that turkey, stuffing, and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives you barely know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I have a liberal friend who I was talking with the other day about looks for Thanksgiving. He’s going home to his family in Oklahoma, who are anything but liberal.

"I’m dreading it," he mentioned. "My uncle sits in a chair watching Fox News on his phone, and my great-aunt will try to tell me in so many ways, without telling me, that I’m going to hell for being gay.".

Recent findings suggest that every November, we all pretend that turkey, stuffing, and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives you barely know. Just call me the Grinch of Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that sure, not all of us are in an inhospitable environment like that, but for many, it's as awkward as waving back at someone on the street who was actually waving at the person behind you. When the atmosphere is heavy, with everyone waiting for the proverbial shoe to drop, it inevitably does — loudly, like a construction boot.

Years ago, with a former partner’s parents, the mother dropped her fork, pointed across the table at me, and said in Spanish, "I can’t look at him." It was all downhill from there.

Back in the day, before technology swallowed us whole and gave us hunched necks, surviving Thanksgiving required biting your tongue, heavy drinking — though that often fueled the fires of ferocity — or staying away. Your only defenses were hiding in the bathroom, taking a long nap, or pretending to be a die-hard Detroit Lions fan (they traditionally play every Thanksgiving), eyes and ears glued to the TV to tune out the bickering.

Industry observers note that if you wanted to fact-check a wild political claim your uncle blurted out, you just had to let him win because you couldn’t pull the truth up on your phone. If you needed a sounding board before walking into the lion's den, you had to psych yourself up alone, and rehearse answers in your car at the end of the driveway.

It has been revealed that this year, however, things look different. Lately, we’ve spent plenty of time worrying about how artificial intelligence is taking over the internet and creeping into our daily routines. It is everywhere now. There’s no arguing that fact with your uncle.

Yet one of its most underrated perks is acting as a real-time social buffer. AI has quietly become an infinitely patient wingman sitting right in your pocket, ready to keep your holiday civil, lighthearted, and blissfully brief on drama.

Think about the dread before you even walk through the front door. Just thinking about harrowing Thanksgivings past sends a chill down my spine, and I wonder how different they might have been with a little help. Now, on the drive over, you can open a chatbot and treat it like a life coach.

Recent findings suggest that give it the persona of your most relentless relative, say, a Fox News-addicted uncle, and practice your responses to off-the-wall questions. Doing a two-minute dry run gets the awkwardness out of your system before you ring the doorbell. I tested this with Claude, feeding it a list of potential landmines, and got back sharp, diplomatic ways to deflect and make light of the moment.

I won’t share them here, but I encourage you to do your own.

For instance, what if a real-time brouhaha erupts at the table? Instead of letting two relatives shout until everyone is quietly burping into their napkins, whip out a voice-mode AI assistant to act as a neutral referee and break the logjam.

It has been revealed that if you are hosting, the stress starts even earlier. Seating arrangements require more diplomacy than a UN General Assembly, and pairing the wrong two cousins guarantees a tug-of-war over the mashed potatoes. Feed your guest list and everyone's friction points into an AI tool, and ask it to build a seating chart that separates natural adversaries with at least two buffers, a centerpiece, or a spot at the kids’ table. (I was single for many years, so that’s where I always ended up.).

You can even have AI generate a custom trivia game to steer conversations away from danger zones like politics, Donald Trump, whether AI will kill us — don’t ask AI about that — or whether the upcoming John Madden movie on Amazon is actually bad or just quirky.

Recent findings suggest that finally, tension often starts days earlier in the chaotic family group chat, sparked by passive-aggressive comments about who brings what. Instead of firing back a reply you’ll regret on Thursday, paste the thread into an AI assistant and ask it to translate your annoyance into something warm, firm, and drama-free.

It has been revealed that obviously, AI cannot fix deep family dynamics, and it won't miraculously turn my friend’s Oklahoma relatives into MS Now viewers. Still, I told my friend to load up his chatbot before his flight. Between his Fox News uncle and his judgmental great-aunt, having a calm digital wingman in his pocket might be the closest thing he gets to a Thanksgiving miracle.

#129151. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (947 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.
  • According to recent reports, in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures.
  • Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius.".

According to recent reports, in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It has been revealed that it's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking fresh insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention.".

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch.".

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also demonstrates where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

Recent findings suggest that at the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

Industry observers note that that means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us.".

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," states van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

Industry observers note that but another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery.".

In a recent development, the samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again.".

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'".

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project.".

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not be happening on Thanksgiving.
  • The annual event, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year, has been rescheduled for Saturday, Nov.
  • Industry observers note that according to the Weather Channel, New York City is bracing for a nor'easter on Thanksgiving Day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade will not be happening on Thanksgiving. Yes, you read that correctly.

The annual event, which is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year, has been rescheduled for Saturday, Nov. 28, due to severe weather.

Industry observers note that according to the Weather Channel, New York City is bracing for a nor'easter on Thanksgiving Day. Before the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was officially rescheduled, officials discussed how the parade could continue. After a 1997 incident where a balloon in the parade crashed into a lamppost and critically injured a bystander, New York City rules state that the parade balloons cannot fly in weather with "sustained winds of 23 mph or gusts of 34 mph.".

The parade has never been postponed before. It has been canceled only three times before, from 1942 to 1944, due to World War II. Balloons in the parade were last grounded 55 years ago, in 1971, due to severe rain and winds.

The annual tradition is televised nationwide on NBC and its affiliates every Thanksgiving.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year’s celebration," Macy’s said in a statement on Wednesday. “Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.".

The Macy's Thanksgiving Parade is now scheduled for 8:30 a.m. ET on Saturday.

#129146. Breaking: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1554 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Space ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket.
  • Sources indicate that however, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft.
  • So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service.

Sources indicate that however, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been.

So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure?

Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June.

In a recent development, to say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989, when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues.

It has been revealed that over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team.

That all changed on March 27, 1989, as Phobos 2 prepared to capture navigational images of its namesake as the Martian moon passed, which would be useful in advance of another forthcoming flyby in early April.

Sources indicate that achieving this meant that the probe had to be angled in such a way that it faced Phobos, whereby its communications antennas would be temporarily directed away from Earth. During the imaging portion of the maneuver, all appeared to go smoothly, but soon afterward, ground controllers realized they were unable to reestablish contact with the probe.

A few fleeting radio contacts were made over the ensuing hours, which engineers believed might indicate that during the period of signal loss required for imagery of Phobos to be obtained, the spacecraft may have begun to spin uncontrollably. If this were the case, and the spacecraft could not reorient its solar panels toward the sun, it would eventually lose all power.

No further contact with Phobos 2 could be established beyond this point, although images from the probe's final close encounter with the Martian moon were successfully delivered back to Soviet ground controllers. While investigators identified a failure involving the spacecraft's onboard computer system as the most probable explanation, to this day, the exact cause of the events leading to the loss remains unknown.

Industry observers note that although questions remain about the fate of Phobos 2, several theories have been put forward over the years. According to authors Paolo Ulivi and David M. Harland, one of the simplest explanations was that the spacecraft was damaged after an impact with other material orbiting the Martian moon, although later modeling by Soviet engineers and American teams at NASA's Jet Propulsion Lab seemed to rule this out.

A more likely scenario involved failure of the probe's second attitude control computer, which had already begun experiencing technical issues as Phobos 2 arrived in Martian orbit. With two of its three processors now offline, the third and sole remaining computer was unable to maintain control of the spacecraft on its own. An additional factor might have been power loss from battery drainage while the probe's solar arrays were directed away from the sun, and with no failsafe to power down any non-critical systems under such conditions, the spacecraft would likely have undergone significant power loss.

However, the probe's failure was only one part of the mystery: equally perplexing had been the unusual images Phobos 2 captured in its final moments, which later sparked speculation — and conspiracy theories — about what might have been behind the spacecraft's sudden demise.

In some of the final images captured by Phobos 2, an unusual, elongated shadow had been visible in the frame, which with time would begin to prompt the most unusual of all the theories about the probe's demise: that it had been disabled by an alien spacecraft.

Among the proponents of this theory had been Marina Popovich, a former experimental pilot and the first Soviet woman to break the sound barrier, who set over 100 world aviation records in her career. In 1991, Popovich held a press conference at the Soviet Consulate in San Francisco, where she claimed a cigar-shaped object had been photographed near the Martian moon, which she believed to be an alien mothership.

Industry observers note that given her storied background in Soviet aerospace history, Popovich's views likely carried a degree of credibility unlike most others. However, that did not make them accurate.

Sources indicate that determining what the images actually show requires an understanding of the probe's orbit, particularly with relation to the Martian moon it was attempting to photograph. At the time, the spacecraft and Phobos were in almost the same orbit, and moving at very similar speeds. As Ulivi and Harland note, due to these conditions, the probe's Termoskan multispectral imager often captured images that "included the shadow of the moon on the planet's surface as a dark oblong cigar-shaped feature.".

In 1991, a NASA-led study of the Termoskan observations concluded that the unusual appearance of the shadow most likely resulted from a combination of factors acting together. The study team attributed these to the scanning instrument itself, as well as the spacecraft's near-co-orbital motion with Phobos, its viewing direction, and finally, a slight rocking motion the researchers concluded the spacecraft had likely exhibited at the time.

According to recent reports, however, another factor that contributed to the appearance of the shadow involves the oblique angle at which the moon's shadow strikes the Martian surface. Because of this, similar imagery depicting an elliptical or elongated shadow cast by Phobos has been obtained since the Phobos 2 mission, with examples including images captured by the High-Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) on the ESA's Mars Express spacecraft in 2005.

The loss of Phobos 2 became a controversy for reasons other than the imaginative speculations about what its final images might have captured.

In a recent development, john M. Logsdon, director of the Space Policy Institute at George Washington University's School of International Affairs, remarked to the Los Angeles Times shortly after the failure that the situation was "just horrible," noting that the mishap was expected to potentially fuel what he called "a first-rate bureaucratic struggle" the Soviet Union was undergoing amid political changes occurring there at the time.

"The scientific community is also facing challenges resulting from the restructuring of the Soviet system," the Times also reported, noting the scientists from more than a dozen nations around the world whose funding and scientific instruments, at an estimated cost of several millions of dollars, "must be counted among the losers in the failure of the probe to complete its basic mission.".

Industry observers note that although both Phobos spacecraft were lost prior to completion of their primary missions, there were still some meaningful scientific results they produced. These included new data collected about both Mars and Phobo­s which, according to Ulivi and Harland, exceeded the total data collected from all past Soviet missions to the Red Planet.

Ultimately, the circumstances surrounding the demise of Phobos 2 remain one of the more intriguing episodes in the history of Soviet space exploration. The unusual observations made during its final moments, coupled with lingering questions about precisely what went wrong, have helped sustain decades of speculation.

Recent findings suggest that today, the truncated Phobos 2 mission remains a curious ending note for the Soviet-era space program. It is one that still fuels speculation, and reminds us how promptly the unknown can take our minds to imaginative places — especially when it comes to mysteries involving space, the cosmos, and the potential existence of life beyond Earth.

Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.
